The Vase tunicate Ciona intestinalis is a globally distributed solitary ascidian that serves as a model organism in developmental biology. Newly settled individuals that have completed metamorphosis and commenced filter-feeding exhibit a total length of approximately 0.1 cm [Lb = approximately 0.1 cm], a value consistent with the size reported for other solitary ascidians at the onset of exogenous feeding and reflecting the minimal structural investment required to commence filter-feeding. Field measurements indicate a typical range of 0.07 to 0.13 cm due to variability at settlement. This modest size at settlement underscores the rapid transition from a free-swimming tadpole larva to a sessile juvenile. Following this initial phase, juveniles enter a period of vigorous somatic growth, ultimately attaining an adult total length of 15 cm [Li = 15 cm] under optimal conditions, a size that distinguishes this species from smaller congeners such as Ciona savignyi and represents a substantial increase from the settlement stage, facilitated by rapid tissue accretion during its relatively brief lifespan.

Reproductive maturity in Ciona intestinalis is achieved at a total length of 5 cm [Lp = 5 cm], a size threshold that signals the onset of gonadal activity. Individuals that have attained this length are capable of producing gametes, marking the transition from a juvenile to a reproductively viable adult. This size-based maturation is ecologically significant, as it ensures that sufficient body volume is available to house the developing gonads and sustain the energetic demands of spawning. The timing of this milestone is closely tied to water temperature, with accelerated development commonly observed under warmer conditions. In laboratory studies conducted at a stable water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], individuals begin to release gametes and engage in their first reproduction event at 60 days after settlement [tR = 60 days after settlement]. This relatively rapid onset of reproduction aligns with the species' opportunistic life-history strategy in temperate fouling communities.

Under the thermal regime of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the embryonic development of Ciona intestinalis proceeds with remarkable speed. The zygote, formed following gamete fusion, undergoes cleavage and organogenesis within a very short timeframe, and the free-swimming tadpole larva hatches at just 1 day after fertilisation [ab = 1 day after fertilisation] at a temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. This accelerated rate of embryogenesis is a defining feature of the species, allowing it to colonise ephemeral substrates effectively. The newly emerged larva, still reliant on endogenous yolk reserves, possesses a rudimentary notochord and a sensory pigment cell that facilitates phototactic behaviour during its brief planktonic phase. Following a short period of swimming, the larva settles and undergoes metamorphosis into a filter-feeding juvenile, a transition that initiates the onset of exogenous feeding. The rapidity of this developmental sequence is an adaptation to the unpredictable and often ephemeral nature of hard-substrate habitats in coastal environments.

The reproductive output of Ciona intestinalis is notably high, reflecting its role as a prolific fouling organism. Laboratory observations at 21 °C [T = 21 °C] have quantified that each spawning event releases approximately 3000 eggs per spawn [N_R_i = approximately 3000 eggs per spawn], a substantial fecundity that is typical of broadcast-spawning ascidians. Furthermore, the species can produce more than one spawn per year, with data indicating roughly 2 to 3 spawning events annually [F_R_i = roughly 2 to 3 spawning events annually], a frequency that aligns with the 2.5 spawnings per year implied by the documented daily reproductive rate. This repeated reproductive effort, combining a large clutch size with a moderate spawning frequency, results in a high annual reproductive capacity that facilitates rapid colonisation of available substrates. The energetic investment per spawn is considerable, and the species relies heavily on stored reserves to support gametogenesis and the subsequent release of gametes into the water column, where fertilisation occurs externally.

Maximum longevity in Ciona intestinalis under controlled laboratory conditions at 21 °C [T = 21 °C] has been recorded as 730 days [am = 730 days], placing this species among the longer-lived solitary ascidians within the family Cionidae, contrasting with the sub-annual lifespans of smaller fouling organisms and reflecting the energetic trade-off between early reproduction and sustained somatic maintenance over two complete annual cycles. Throughout this period, individuals maintain their sessile lifestyle, continuously filtering planktonic particles from the water column via their pharyngeal basket. The eventual death of the organism is typically associated with senescence and progressive physiological deterioration rather than predation, although the species is subject to grazing pressure from nudibranchs and other benthic predators. The relatively short lifespan, coupled with early reproductive maturation and high fecundity, defines a life-history strategy that is well-suited to fluctuating environments where colonisation ability is at a premium.
